name: Interstitial Lung Disease & Pulmonary Fibrosis
cards: Interstitial lung disease is characterized by?
Scarring (fibrosis) and/or inflammation of the lungs.
Lung region involved in interstitial lung disease?
Parenchyma: alveoli, alveolar ducts, respiratory bronchioles.
Most common presenting complaint in interstitial lung disease?
Shortness of breath.
Why do fibrotic lungs fail to expand?
Scarred tissue becomes stiff and restrictive.
Cells that gather in alveolar walls before fibrosis?
Macrophages, lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils.
Alveolitis leads to?
Production of fibroblasts.
What directly causes the fibrosis?
Collagen produced in the lung.
Most common interstitial lung disease of known etiology?
Occupational or environmental exposure (inorganic dusts, organic dusts, fumes or gases).
Treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease?
Radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, chemotherapy.
Autoimmune drug that can itself cause interstitial lung disease?
Methotrexate, used for lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
Acute interstitial lung disease presentation?
Days to weeks; occurs with allergy.
Subacute presentation (weeks to months) is most common with?
Sarcoidosis and drug-induced interstitial lung disease.
How do most interstitial lung diseases present?
Chronically, over months to years.
Interstitial lung disease that can present episodically?
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, a less common pattern.
Classic interstitial lung disease symptoms?
Progressive exertional dyspnea or persistent nonproductive cough.
Interstitial lung disease lung exam?
Bibasilar dry rales (inspiratory crackles) and small lung volumes.
Advanced interstitial lung disease heart finding?
Right heart failure.
High antinuclear antibody in interstitial lung disease suggests?
Collagen vascular disease.
Anti-glomerular and anti-alveolar basement membrane antibodies suggest?
Goodpasture syndrome (lung hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis).
Eosinophilia in interstitial lung disease suggests?
Eosinophilic pneumonia, sarcoidosis, or drug-induced disease.
Hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on chest film suggests?
Sarcoidosis or silicosis.
Ground-glass (fine reticular) opacity: early or late?
An early finding.
Honeycombing (medium reticular): early or late?
A late finding.
Interstitial lung disease pulmonary function pattern?
Restrictive, with reduced lung volumes.
Restrictive pattern: 1-second volume to forced vital capacity ratio?
Normal or increased.
Restrictive pattern: total lung capacity and forced vital capacity?
Both are decreased.
Most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia subtype?
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Smoking history in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
67% to 75% of patients.
Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia symptoms?
Insidious dry cough, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, malaise.
Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia exam findings?
Clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea, reduced chest expansion.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis computed tomography?
Diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing.
Who can skip surgical lung biopsy for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
Over 65 with all four classic features.
Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia management?
Controversial; nothing improves survival over no treatment.
Key step to prolong life in idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia?
Smoking cessation is critical.

name: Sarcoidosis
cards: Cause of sarcoidosis?
Unknown; it is idiopathic.
Sarcoidosis hallmark pathology?
Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation.
Cells that make up a granuloma?
T lymphocytes, macrophages, epithelioid cells.
Organs sarcoidosis affects most often?
The lungs and lymphatic system.
Proposed trigger of sarcoidosis?
Environmental trigger in a genetically predisposed person.
Share of sarcoidosis with lung granulomas?
About 90% of patients.
Populations with higher sarcoidosis occurrence?
North American Black and Northern European white people.
Sex more often affected by sarcoidosis?
More often affects women.
Sarcoidosis age of onset?
Third and fourth decades of life.
Sarcoidosis dyspnea onset pattern?
Insidious onset.
Sarcoidosis lymph nodes?
Enlarged but nontender lymph nodes.
Sarcoidosis facial skin lesion?
Lupus pernio (painful skin sores on the face).
Lupus pernio with a dry cough suggests?
Points to sarcoidosis.
Sarcoidosis rash on the lower legs?
Erythema nodosum (painful rash on lower legs and ankles).
Sarcoidosis gland finding?
Parotid gland enlargement.
Sarcoidosis abdominal organ findings?
Liver and spleen enlargement.
Sarcoidosis chest film?
Symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy.
Sarcoidosis lab findings?
Leukopenia, eosinophilia, elevated sedimentation rate, hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme in sarcoidosis?
Elevated in 40% to 80% of patients.
Hypercalcemia frequency in sarcoidosis?
About 5% of patients.
Increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate in interstitial lung disease suggests?
Points to active sarcoidosis.
Test that confirms sarcoidosis?
Transbronchial or fine-needle node biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas.
Sarcoidosis stage I chest film?
Bilateral hilar adenopathy alone.
Sarcoidosis stage II chest film?
Hilar adenopathy plus parenchymal involvement.
Sarcoidosis stage III chest film?
Parenchymal involvement alone (diffuse reticular infiltrates).
Sarcoidosis stage IV chest film?
Advanced fibrosis with honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts.
When is biopsy essential in suspected sarcoidosis?
When an alternative such as lymphoma is possible.
Sarcoidosis treatment to which about 90% of cases respond?
Corticosteroids.
Sarcoidosis therapy when steroids fail or are not tolerated?
Methotrexate, azathioprine, or infliximab.
Sarcoidosis laboratory abnormality that is an indication for oral corticosteroids?
Hypercalcemia.
Sarcoidosis skin lesion that alone is not an oral steroid indication?
Erythema nodosum (lower-leg rash).
Best sarcoidosis prognosis?
Hilar adenopathy alone.
Worse sarcoidosis prognosis?
Parenchymal lung involvement on imaging.
Irreversible lung impairment in sarcoidosis with lung involvement?
About 20% of patients.
Yearly sarcoidosis monitoring?
Exam, pulmonary function, chest film, electrocardiogram, chemistry panel, eye exam.
Why a yearly eye exam in sarcoidosis?
To find and manage ocular inflammation.

name: Occupational Lung Disease
cards: Pneumoconiosis definition?
Chronic fibrotic lung disease from inhaled coal or inorganic dust.
How do coal macules form?
Alveolar macrophages take up inhaled coal dust.
Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
Usually asymptomatic; pulmonary function can be unimpressive.
Complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
Progressive massive fibrosis.
Where does progressive massive fibrosis form?
Upper lung fields, with conglomeration and contraction.
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis chest film?
Upper-field nodular opacities (coal macules 2 to 5 mm).
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis pulmonary function?
Restrictive, with reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide.
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis treatment?
Supportive care; no curative treatment exists.
Coal miner with small upper-field nodules?
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis.
Asbestos exposure settings?
Insulation, demolition, shipyards, construction.
Tissue finding of significant asbestos exposure?
Ferruginous bodies in tissue.
Ferruginous bodies result from?
Inhalation of inorganic dust.
Smoking plus asbestos exposure?
Markedly increases lung cancer incidence.
Asbestosis symptoms?
Exertional dyspnea; cough is rare.
Asbestosis pulmonary function?
Reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity.
Most common asbestos chest film finding?
Pleural plaques on the chest film.
Preferred imaging for asbestosis?
Computed tomography scan.
Shipyard insulation worker with pleural plaques?
Asbestosis from asbestos fibers.
What is mesothelioma?
Primarily cancer of the pleural lining.
Cause of mesothelioma?
Nearly always asbestos exposure.
How is mesothelioma often diagnosed?
Pleural fluid cytology from an effusion.
Silicosis exposures?
Mining, sandblasting, quarry work, stone work.
Why does silica reach the upper lobes?
It is a lighter dust.
Silicosis bronchoalveolar lavage?
Thick, milky fluid with foamy macrophages.
Silicosis hilar node finding?
Eggshell calcification of the node periphery.
Infection risk in silicosis?
Increased tuberculosis risk.
Screening for patients with silicosis?
Tuberculosis skin test and current chest film.
Sandblaster with eggshell hilar calcification?
Silicosis from silica dust.
Other name for hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis.
Cause of hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
Inhaled organic dust.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis sources?
Moldy hay, bird excreta, feathers, moldy sugarcane, insect-infested grain.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis nausea timing?
4 to 8 hours after exposure.
Acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis onset?
Within 9 hours of exposure.
Definitive hypersensitivity pneumonitis test?
Serum antibodies to the agent.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis histology?
Lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrates with noncaseating granulomas.
Key hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatment?
Identify and avoid the agent.
Bird keeper with fever and cough hours after exposure?
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (bird fancier's lung).

name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
cards: Major systemic triggers of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Sepsis, severe pancreatitis, shock, nonthoracic trauma.
Direct pulmonary insults causing acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Gastric aspiration, diffuse pneumonia, lung contusion.
Drug overdoses that can precipitate acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Opioids, aspirin, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants, cocaine.
Iatrogenic and blood risks for acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Multiple transfusions, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cardiopulmonary bypass, protamine.
Drugs whose lung toxicity can cause acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Chemotherapy, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin.
Toxic gases that cause acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Chlorine, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ammonia, smoke.
Embolic causes of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Fat, air, amniotic fluid, or thrombus emboli.
Environmental causes of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Near-drowning, high altitude, radiation, upper airway obstruction.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome mortality with low tidal volume ventilation?
About 30% overall.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome mortality by cause?
20% in trauma to 80% in end-stage liver disease.
Lung function recovery after acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Improves over 6 to 12 months.
Result of increased vascular permeability in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Surfactant loss, alveolar collapse, refractory hypoxemia.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome onset criterion?
Within 7 days of a known clinical insult.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome imaging criterion?
Bilateral opacities not explained by effusion, atelectasis, or nodules.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome origin criterion?
Not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome oxygenation criterion?
Arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen fraction ratio under 300 mm Hg.
Mild acute respiratory distress syndrome oxygenation ratio?
200 to 300 mm Hg.
Moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome oxygenation ratio?
100 to 200 mm Hg.
Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome oxygenation ratio?
Below 100 mm Hg.
Dyspnea onset after the insult in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
12 to 48 hours.
Hallmark hypoxemia of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Refractory to supplemental oxygen.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome exam signs?
Tachypnea, labored breathing, intercostal retractions, crackles.
Heart size on imaging in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Normal, with minimal or absent effusions.
Echocardiogram role in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Exclude cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Differential with cardiomegaly and batwing perihilar opacities?
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Ventilator strategy in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Low tidal volumes.
Positive end-expiratory pressure goal in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Arterial oxygen tension above 60 mm Hg.
Positioning that lowers mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Early prone positioning.
Ventilation mode to avoid in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation.
Fluid strategy in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Conservative: central venous pressure under 4 mm Hg.
Transfusion threshold in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Hemoglobin of 7 g/dL.
Routine pulmonary artery catheter in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Avoid; no clinical benefit.
Corticosteroids in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Guidelines conditionally support them within 14 days.
Neuromuscular blockade in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Controversial; trials conflict on mortality benefit.
Salvage therapy for severe refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome?
ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).
Lasting deficits after acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Diffusion deficits, muscle wasting, weakness, fatigue.
